newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets suffer as Iraq exports approach.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets suffer as Iraq exports approach.

text.p: Oil prices fell on Friday as Iraq got the final go-ahead from the United Nations to resume the sale of crude.
Speculators baled out of crude futures in the expectation that Baghdad will be exporting oil by next week, saturating the market with extra supply.
North Sea Brent blend futures for September have lost a dollar since Monday and were trading down 20 cents in London at $18.70 a barrel at 1600 gmt.

Iraq's pricing formula for oil exports in the second phase of the oil-for-food deal with the U.N. was given formal Security Council approval, leaving Baghdad free to sell crude again after a delay since the end of May.
Tankers chartered to load Iraqi oil from outlets on the Mediterranean and the Gulf are expected to start sailing by the end of next week.
Dealers said a reversal in strong U.S. and European gasoline markets had coincided with progress on Iraqi sales and had helped undermine crude values.
European gasoline plummeted $13 a tonne on Friday as Wall Street trader Morgan Stanley stepped out of a market it had squeezed higher.
But most traders were not anticpating a heavy slide in oil prices, which touched a low for the year at $17.30 a barrel in early June.
The West's energy watchdog, the International Energy Agency, said on Friday that world oil markets had proved more resilient than expected this year.

"Oil markets were much tighter than expected in June and July as the absence of Iraqi exports was compounded by supply shortfalls from several areas and strong demand," the agency said in its monthly Oil Market Report.

Commercial oil stocks held in Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries rose by just 480,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the second quarter of the year, the smallest second quarter increase since the 1991 Gulf War, the Paris-based IEA said.
The agency made hefty downward revisions to its non-OPEC supply forecast, cutting an average of almost 500,000 barrels a day (bpd) from previous estimates through to the end of 1998.
It said lower projections for non-OPEC supply reflected "the recent underperformance in the North Sea and Australia," and downward revisions to data for some developing countries.
